So my current group is starting a new campaign in a world we've been playing in the past couple adventures. we've got a bit of lore, but really only enough for the relevant two adventures we had gone through. Any tips for really fleshing out worlds?

This is a tough question to answer as it is very broad. I will say that you don't necessarily have to flesh out an entire world to continue playing, just have some rough ideas written down to build off of later. For example, you could draw an entire globe of your world (or flat plane depending on what type of world it is :D ) with just the basic details filled in like continents and oceans; then you can pick an area to start and slowly begin filling in the details as your adventurers begin exploring. This allows you to have an idea of what to expect later on but you only have to spend a few minutes drawing the rough outlines instead of months on every mountain range, river, capital city, kingdom, etc. There are endless details you could get into for each aspect of a customized world but 99% of the time your players will never ask or encounter the detail you worked so hard on which can be frustrating.

The same goes for other parts of the world. You can write down some faction/cult names and some bullet points on them like their ultimate goal and motive to use when appropriate. Jot down some possible world-changing events that could occur and when things get slow throw one in to shake things up. If you have some ideas in the back of your mind about plots, adventures or story lines then take a minute to write them all down somewhere handy so you can refer back to them. Over time you can find unique and inspiring ways to link things together based on how your players do things.

Think about designing a puzzle. You might spend days or even weeks trying to come up with the perfect solution for your players to figure out or you could put some things around the room that seem intentional and let the players come up with something completely unique as they try to figure out how everything fits together. Both options work, it just depends on how much time you want to put in.

Good luck with your campaign! World building can be a lot of fun :)

Thanks. I'll go over stuff like this with the others involved in the world creation (i.e. the authors of the group) and see what we can come up with on this. The plan is to flesh out as much as possible, as this latest campaign is latest down the story line (~100 yrs. after the last campaign), So perhaps I'll come up with some other adventures for later that we can fill in the holes with, and just put them in vaguely, so that more personal decisions aren't locked in. (Similar to how the Elder Scrolls handles it's lore)

When I created my first world I made a map, plotted down some towns that made sense, and then figured out how far back in lore I'd like to go. The current age of my world is around 850, or really the amount of time that has past since the "volcano" destroyed the land and sea. Few relics of the past age can be found and are greatly celebrated and sought after once found. The big bad evil guy in this world currently is trying to resurrect some great ancient evil from the past to rule this new world.

I've only created one homebrew world but it's gotten large and detailed over time, which has been a fantastic experience I have thoroughly enjoyed. Here's my list of tips, to be taken with a grain of salt since I'm new to DM'ing in relativity to some of the true grognards out there.

  1. Think historically. I started my universe by drawing a map at random and then arbitrarily creating cities and nations. After that, I started thinking about the long term history of each of these places, and their relationships with each other. It's easy to flesh out NPC's and their motivations if you have a little bit of the history of their community developed.

  2. The tides of conflict I think it's extremely helpful to your ability to create compelling places/things/people on the fly if you have an overarching event brewing. There should be a few key players you've created or at least places with motivations. Something needs to be HAPPENING in the world. In my campaign, an ancient black dragon is awakening deep underground after a 4000 year rest. Nobody has seen a dragon since he crawled under the earth and was buried there by the Dao he was assaulting. There's a queen who has ruled over a thriving city in the mountains for 4000 years. Everyone believes she's a magical witch of some sort and never ages, but she is kind and caring to her people so she is worshiped and revered by them. She's actually an ancient silver dragon, and 4000 years ago she tricked the black dragon into digging his way to his own doom. This is setting up a CONFLICT somewhere down the line. Not sure how that will play out, but it gives me something to hint towards, and to develop slowly, which makes it easier to create NPC's and interesting dialogue, becuase I have a conflict brewing in the world behind the scenes that players don't know about. This is just one of about 8 major conflicts I have going on all over my land, some involving gods, some involving nations, some involving individuals. It's nice to set points and counter-points all over your map at the beginning, so that you can watch your players walk through the strings that are connecting these conflicts and hopefully entice them to eventually get involved. I think 8 is overkill, but I've had a lot of time to develop. Start with one brewing conflict and go from there.

  3. Don't stress Most of the best parts of my universe were created on the fly during sessions. Usually I would have the time to set up a detailed environment for the session, complete with planned NPC's, dialogue, dungeon schematics, and major story-arc elements. Other times though, I had no time to set up anything. I wouldn't tell my players that, but I would just go with the flow and use my context of brewing conflicts and world history to make shit up. Some of the best sessions were these types of sessions. Being comfortable to create your world with your players on the fly is the most important part of homebrew, and the most rewarding.

  4. Take good session notes I suck at this, and as a result I have lost track of certain things that happen during sessions that may have had profound effects on the world. I think that thorough notes on what happens allows you to take things players did and make them have long term effects. There's nothing better as a player than finding out 6 months after you stabbed some seemingly meaningless NPC that his dad is a prince and you've got an army chasing you. Bringing consequences and effects to your players actions make the world much more engaging, and you must take good notes to do so. (or have a better memory than a lump of dirt, which I personally do not.)
Also check out /v/worldbuilding for plenty of discussion specifically on world creation!
